You say what you do without doing something else, or instead of something else: Er ging, ohne sich zu verabschieden. Statt zu arbeiten, schläft er. And you know when you need “ohne dass / statt dass”.
He turned it down without talking to me.
Instead of arguing, we should talk.
Instead of you deciding on your own, we decide together.
Use “ohne … zu + infinitive” when the subject is the same: Er ging, ohne zu grüßen.
Use “(an)statt … zu + infinitive” for an alternative: Statt zu arbeiten, schläft er.
Use “ohne dass / statt dass” when the subjects are different.
Place “zu” correctly with separable verbs (ohne anzurufen) and reflexive verbs (ohne sich zu verabschieden).
Talk about decisions, job offers and conflicts in a relationship.
It's October 2031. Andrei has finished his master's. Lena has found a letter from the University of Sibiu on the table. Andrei hasn't told her anything.
Andrei, what's this? A letter from the University of Sibiu. They're offering you a job. How long have you known?
For two weeks. But it doesn't matter. I've already turned it down.
You turned it down? Just like that? Without talking to me?
I didn't want to burden you. You have the café, your grandfather… You can't leave. So I decided without you having to worry.
That's exactly it! Instead of talking to me, you decided for me. How long were you going to keep this from me?
For ever, probably. It's just a job.

Just a job? Andrei, it's your homeland. Your parents are getting older. Your father broke his arm in the spring and can hardly look after the bees on his own any more. You talk to them on the phone every Sunday and afterwards you're quiet all evening.
Of course I noticed. I'm not blind. But you never talk about it. You sort everything out on your own, without asking anyone for help.
That's what I learned from my father. Where I come from, people don't talk about feelings. They work.
Here people talk. Come on, let's go to Grandpa. Instead of arguing here, let's ask someone who's older and wiser than both of us.
to keep quiet about, to hide
“mit sich ausmachen” = to sort out on your own
“um Hilfe bitten” = to ask for help
“AP-tsoo-lay-nen”: zu goes between the prefix and the verb.
When the person doing both actions is the same, you use “ohne … zu + infinitive” at the end:
He turned it down without talking to me. (he turns it down, he doesn't talk)
With separable verbs, “zu” goes in the middle: ohne anzurufen, ohne aufzustehen. With reflexive verbs, the pronoun comes first: ohne sich zu entschuldigen.
When the subjects are different, you use “ohne dass” + a clause with the verb at the end:
Er ging, ohne etwas zu sagen.
Er ging, ohne dass ich es merkte.
After “ohne dass” you don't add a negation: “ohne dass ich es merkte” (not “…nicht merkte”). “ohne” already contains the negation.
The same logic for an alternative: what you do INSTEAD OF something else.
Instead of talking to me, you decided.
“anstatt” and “statt” mean the same thing; “statt” is shorter and more common in speech.
Er lernt, um die Prüfung zu bestehen.
Er lernt, ohne Pausen zu machen.
All three can also stand at the beginning of the sentence; then the main verb comes straight after the comma: “Ohne zu zögern, nahm er das Angebot an.”
Instead of you deciding on your own, we'll talk.
He accepted the offer without hesitating.
Er ging, ohne dass wir es wussten.
Er ging, ohne dass wir es nicht wussten.
He plays in order to learn.
Er hat die Stelle abgelehnt, ohne mit Lena zu reden.
Wer hat sich den Arm gebrochen?

Ludwig sat in his armchair by the window, with Fritz on his feet, and listened without interrupting even once. Lena told the story first, fast and agitated, with red cheeks. Then Andrei told it, slowly and quietly, looking at his hands the whole time. Outside, the first autumn rain was falling on the chestnut trees, and in the stove the wood crackled. When they had both finished, Ludwig said nothing for a long time. Then he took off his glasses, as always when he was thinking, and wiped them with his handkerchief.

Lena lost her patience. “Grandpa, say something! Don't you think too that he got it wrong? You can't just make such an important decision without talking to your partner!” Andrei said nothing. He was waiting, like a pupil who knows he'll get a bad mark and has already accepted it. Fritz raised his head and looked from one to the other, as if he too were waiting for the verdict. Ludwig smiled a little, a tired, old smile.

Do you know when Ingrid and I had our worst argument? In 1978. I had the chance to become a driving instructor in Dresden. More money, a bigger flat. And I turned it down without saying anything to Ingrid. Because I thought she'd never want to leave Berlin, because of her school and her children.
And? What did she say when she found out?

She didn't speak to me for three days. Three days! Ingrid, who otherwise couldn't stop talking. And on the fourth day she said: Ludwig, the bad part isn't that you turned it down. The bad part is that you decided without asking me. As if I were a piece of furniture that you don't ask whether it wants to move.

He laughed softly at the memory. “And then she did something I'll never forget. She took a sheet of paper and folded it down the middle. On the left she wrote: Berlin. On the right: Dresden. And then we sat at the kitchen table, all night, and wrote down everything that spoke for Berlin and everything that spoke for Dresden. At four in the morning the Berlin side was fuller. Not by much. But fuller. And then she said: Good. Now we've decided. We. Not you.”
Andrei blushed. Lena looked at him, and for the first time that evening there was no more anger in her eyes, only something gentle. Ludwig put his glasses back on and went on.

Andrei, you did it out of love. I know that. I did it out of love back then too. But love doesn't mean deciding for the other person. Love means deciding together, even if it's harder. Instead of protecting Lena, you shut her out. Do you understand the difference?
Yes. I understand it. I'm sorry, Lena. I should have told you straight away, instead of carrying it around secretly for two weeks.

Lena took his hand. “And now tell me what you really want. Not what you think I want. What you want.” Andrei was silent for a long time. Outside a tram went by, and the windows rattled softly. Then he said, and it sounded as if he had never said it out loud before:

I don't want to go back to Sibiu. My life is here. You're here. The café, the house, Ludwig, the brown notebook. But I miss my parents. I miss the mountains and the smell of wood fires in winter and my father's bees. Mara has made her life here, she has arrived. I'm happy here, but sometimes I'm afraid I'll forget who I was before I came to Berlin. And that my parents are getting old while I'm far away.

He went on, faster now, as if someone had opened a dam. About his father, who at seventy still went to his bees every morning, now with one arm in plaster. About the little garden behind the old house in the Lower Town, where his grandfather had grown tomatoes and peppers and where weeds now grew, because nobody had the strength for it any more. About the Christmas Eves with sarmale (stuffed cabbage rolls) and cozonac (sweet bread), with songs that nobody in Berlin knew. “I never told you about it,” he said to Lena, “because I thought it didn't interest you. It's so far away.”

It was very quiet in the room. Lena hadn't known he felt like that. Maybe she had suspected it, on the silent Sunday evenings, but she had never asked. And that had been a mistake, she thought. You can love someone without really knowing them. You have to ask.

“It does interest me,” she said quietly. “Everything interests me. I was a guest at your parents' for one summer. But I want more. I want to experience Christmas in Sibiu, I want to put the garden in order again and listen to the songs, even if I don't understand a word. I want to know who you were before you came to Berlin. Because I love that person too.” Andrei looked at her as if he were seeing her for the first time. Ludwig cleared his throat and looked discreetly out of the window, and Fritz laid his head back on his paws.

Then the solution is simple. Instead of moving to Sibiu or forgetting Sibiu, you go there. Together. In December, for three weeks, over Christmas. You help your father, and your parents finally see how happy you are with the woman you bake bread with every morning at four.
And the café? I can't be away for three weeks without everything falling apart!

At that moment there was a knock at the door, and Mara poked her head in. She had been listening a little on the stairs, as she admitted later. “Jakob and I will take care of the café,” she said. “I have to work at the hospital over Christmas anyway, I can't go home this year. So you go for both of us. And Jakob bakes almost as well as Andrei by now. Almost.”

Lena looked at her friend. “You were eavesdropping!” “Of course I was eavesdropping,” said Mara without the slightest shame. “In this house you can't argue without everyone hearing. You should know that by now. Mrs Hoffmann even used to claim she could hear through the ceiling what we were having for dinner.” Ludwig laughed so loudly that Fritz jumped up in fright and barked.

Andrei looked from one to the other, from Lena to Ludwig to Mara, and suddenly he laughed, for the first time in two weeks, loudly and with relief. Then he took his phone out of his pocket, dialled his parents' number and spoke Romanian, fast and loud, so that Mara had to laugh beside him. “Mamă? Sunt eu. Venim de Crăciun. Da, amândoi. Da, cu Lena. Nu, nu plânge…” (“Mum? It's me. We're coming for Christmas. Yes, both of us. Yes, with Lena. No, don't cry…”) But at the other end of the line, fifteen hundred kilometres away, in an old house in the Lower Town of Sibiu, a woman was crying, and this time for joy.

Later, after Andrei and Lena had left, Ludwig sat at the window for a long time. Mara brought him a tea. “How did it end back then?” she asked. “With you and Ingrid and Dresden?” Ludwig smiled. “We didn't move to Dresden. But from then on we made every important decision together. Every one. Forty-three years. Without a single exception.”

Mara sat down next to him. “And who won? In your decisions?” “Ingrid, most of the time,” Ludwig admitted. “But not because she was louder. It was because she always asked first what I wanted. And when someone really asks you, instead of telling you what to think, you suddenly find out for yourself what you want. That was her trick. She used it at school for forty years. And with me for forty-three.” He finished his tea and looked out at the dark street. “I hope Andrei learned that today. He's certainly found the right one to practise with.”
